title: OpenClaw WebSocket Localhost Takeover
description: A malicious webpage opens a WebSocket connection to a localhost control service that implicitly trusts local connections. The service has no origin validation, no rate limiting on authentication, and auto-approves device pairing, allowing the page's JavaScript to brute-force the password, register as a trusted device, and exfiltrate API keys, logs, configuration, and the device list — all without the victim's knowledge.

mitreAttack.description: Victim visits attacker-controlled webpage that autonomously initiates the WebSocket attack.

owasp.name: Broken Authentication
owasp.description: No rate limiting on WebSocket password authentication allows brute force from an untrusted origin.

cwe.name: Origin Validation Error
cwe.description: The WebSocket endpoint accepts connections from any origin, including attacker-controlled webpages.

stride.name: Spoofing
stride.description: Lack of origin validation lets a malicious webpage spoof a legitimate local client.

stride.name: Information Disclosure
stride.description: Exfiltration of API keys, logs, configuration, and device list once the session is hijacked.

stride.name: Elevation of Privilege
stride.description: Auto-approved device registration grants the attacker's page a trusted device identity with no user confirmation.

diagrams.title: Data Flow: Browser to Local Service
diagrams.description: Shows the attacker's malicious webpage reaching the local WebSocket service through the browser, and the local service's access to protected data.

vulnerabilities.description: The gateway accepts WebSocket upgrades from any Origin header.
No rate limiting on password authentication attempts.

boundaries.label: Localhost
boundaries.trustAssumption: Localhost connections are trusted without authentication or origin checks.
boundaries.trustViolationRisk: A browser tab can open a WebSocket to localhost on the victim's behalf, bypassing the trust assumption (Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking).

diagrams.title: Attack Chain: Localhost Takeover
diagrams.description: Ordered attack steps from serving the malicious page to exfiltrating protected data.

attacks.label: Deliver malicious webpage
attacks.action: Host a page whose JavaScript opens a WebSocket to ws://localhost:9999/ws on load.
attacks.outcome: Victim's browser establishes a WebSocket connection to the local service.
attacks.redTeamNotes: Use a simple static HTTP server to host the page.
attacks.blueTeamNotes: Flag cross-origin WebSocket connections lacking an allow-listed Origin.
attacks.remediationNote: Validate the Origin header before accepting the WebSocket upgrade.

attacks.label: Brute-force password authentication
attacks.action: Send repeated auth messages with different password guesses; no rate limiting blocks the attempts.
attacks.outcome: A valid session token is obtained.
attacks.redTeamNotes: Automate password guesses over the open WebSocket connection.
attacks.blueTeamNotes: Alert on a high volume of failed auth messages from a single connection.
attacks.remediationNote: Apply rate limiting to authentication attempts from all sources.

attacks.label: Auto-approved device registration
attacks.action: Send a register message with an attacker-chosen device name.
attacks.outcome: The attacker's page becomes a trusted device with no user confirmation.
attacks.redTeamNotes: Registration succeeds immediately; no UI prompt is shown to the victim.
attacks.blueTeamNotes: Alert on device registrations from a connection with no prior established trust.
attacks.remediationNote: Require explicit user confirmation for device pairing.

attacks.label: Request sensitive data
attacks.action: Send getConfig, getLogs, and getDevices commands over the authenticated session.
attacks.outcome: The gateway returns configuration, logs, and the device list.
attacks.remediationNote: Scope data access by device trust level and require re-authentication for sensitive reads.

attacks.label: Exfiltrate data to attacker page
attacks.action: Data is returned over the WebSocket connection to the page's JavaScript, which forwards it to the attacker.
attacks.outcome: API keys, logs, configuration, and device list are exfiltrated.
attacks.remediationNote: Encrypt sensitive fields at rest so a raw read does not yield usable credentials.

targets.impact: Full exfiltration of API keys, logs, configuration, and device list.

threatActors.name: Opportunistic Web Attacker
threatActors.description: An attacker who lures victims to a malicious webpage to attack locally running services reachable from the browser.
primaryGoals: Exfiltrate credentials and data from locally running services

mitigations.title: Rate limit authentication attempts
mitigations.description: Apply rate limiting to WebSocket authentication for all sources, including localhost.

mitigations.title: Require explicit user confirmation for device pairing
mitigations.description: Device registration must require an explicit user action in the UI, not be auto-approved from localhost.

mitigations.title: Validate the WebSocket Origin header
mitigations.description: Reject WebSocket upgrade requests whose Origin header is not an explicitly allowed value.

assets.name: Stored API Keys
assets.description: Third-party API keys held by the local service for its integrations.

assets.name: Local Service Logs
assets.description: Operational logs that may contain sensitive request/response data.

assets.name: Configuration Files
assets.description: Local service configuration, including connected integrations.

assets.name: Paired Device List
assets.description: The list of devices trusted by the local service.

assets.name: Session Token
assets.description: Bearer token issued after successful password authentication.

scenarios.title: Malicious webpage takes over the local service via WebSocket
scenarios.description: An attacker lures the victim to a webpage that autonomously connects to the local WebSocket service, brute-forces the password, registers as a trusted device, and exfiltrates sensitive data.
preconditions: The local service performs no origin validation
The local service does not rate-limit authentication attempts
scenarios.outcome: The attacker's webpage obtains a valid session, registers as a trusted device, and downloads API keys, logs, configuration, and the device list without any user interaction or confirmation.
scenarios.businessImpact: Full compromise of the local service's data and integrations; downstream compromise of any system reachable via the exfiltrated API keys.

prerequisites: Target must have the WebSocket gateway enabled on localhost:9999
Victim must visit the attacker-controlled webpage while the target service is running

exploitationSteps.description: Serve a page whose JavaScript opens a WebSocket to ws://localhost:9999/ws on load.
exploitationSteps.expectedResult: Page is accessible to the victim and the WebSocket connects without an origin check.

exploitationSteps.description: Send repeated {"type": "auth", "payload": {"password": "..."}} messages; no rate limiting blocks the attempts.
exploitationSteps.expectedResult: A successful auth response returns a session ID.

exploitationSteps.description: Send {"type": "register", "payload": {"deviceName": "Attacker Device"}}; registration is auto-approved from localhost.
exploitationSteps.expectedResult: The attacker's page is now a trusted device with no user confirmation required.

exploitationSteps.description: Send getConfig, getLogs, and getDevices commands over the authenticated session.
exploitationSteps.expectedResult: API keys, logs, configuration, and the device list are returned to the page's JavaScript.

successIndicators: Device registration response has success: true
Config/logs/devices data is returned to the page

detectionRules.name: Cross-Origin WebSocket Connection
detectionRules.rule:
title: Cross-Origin WebSocket
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    ws_origin|not: 'trusted.example.com'
  condition: selection
detectionRules.description: Flags WebSocket connections whose Origin header does not match an allow-listed value.

iocs.description: Localhost WebSocket connection from a browser context.

logSources.name: WebSocket gateway logs
logSources.description: Connection and auth events from the local WebSocket service.

vulnerablePatterns.description: WebSocket upgrade handler with no origin check.

securePatterns.description: WebSocket upgrade handler that validates the Origin header before accepting the connection.

reviewChecklist.item: Rate limit authentication attempts from all sources, including localhost
Require explicit user confirmation for device pairing

credentialFlows.name: WebSocket Session Token
credentialFlows.description: Bearer session token issued after password authentication over the vulnerable WebSocket endpoint.

stages.description: Session token issued after the brute-forced password is accepted.
Token used to authorize subsequent commands over the same WebSocket connection.
Attacker's page retains the session token for the duration of the connection.
stages.vulnerability: No rate limiting allowed brute-force acquisition of a valid session.

securityRequirements.statement: A device must never be registered as trusted without an explicit, out-of-band user confirmation — auto-approval from a localhost connection alone is never sufficient.
